Indigenous Peoples of the Americas. The diverse civilizations and societies inhabiting North and South America before European contact, numbering in the tens of millions. These peoples had developed sophisticated cultures, technologies, and political systems ranging from vast empires like the Aztec and Inca to smaller nations and tribes. European colonization initiated by figures like Christopher Columbus devastated these populations through disease, warfare, and subjugation, fundamentally transforming the hemisphere. Indigenous peoples inhabited the Americas for at least fifteen thousand years, with some evidence suggesting twenty thousand or more, having migrated from Asia across the Bering Strait during the last ice age. They developed the hemisphere independently of Old World influence. They created independent civilizations: the Aztec Empire in Mesoamerica, the Inca Empire spanning the length of South America, and hundreds of distinct nations north of Mexico ranging from the Iroquois Confederacy to the Mississippian culture. These peoples possessed advanced knowledge in agriculture, domesticating maize, potatoes, chocolate, and tomatoes. They excelled in astronomy, with Mayan calendars of extraordinary precision. They created monumental architecture including pyramid temples and stone fortifications. They engineered suspension bridges, canal systems, and agricultural terracing. European contact initiated by Christopher Columbus in fourteen ninety-two led to catastrophic demographic collapse, primarily through disease—smallpox, measles, influenza—but also through warfare, forced labor, and famine from disrupted food systems. Population estimates at contact ranged from fifty to one hundred million. Indigenous populations declined by ninety percent within the first century of colonization, representing one of history's deadliest catastrophes, mostly from disease unintentionally spread by Europeans. Colonial powers imposed their religions, languages, legal systems, and labor hierarchies including encomienda and plantation slavery, destroying traditional cultures, political structures, and knowledge systems. Forced conversions and suppression of indigenous religions lasted centuries. Despite genocidal policies, indigenous peoples survived and persisted. Modern indigenous nations, over one thousand recognized groups, continue to claim territorial rights, preserve languages and traditions, and assert political autonomy. Indigenous peoples constitute over six hundred million people globally today.
